sentences.nl: Vandaag oefenen we zinnen, met de grammatica van #dutchgrammar les 38, over vaste combinaties van werkwoorden en preposities.
sentences.en: Today we practice sentences with the grammar from #dutchgrammar lesson 38, about fixed combinations of verbs and prepositions.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Today practice we sentences, with the grammar of #dutchgrammar lesson 38, about fixed combinations of verbs and prepositions.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Vandaag oefenen we" follows the standard Dutch word order for main clauses: time (Vandaag) - verb (oefenen) - subject (we).  
• "vaste combinaties" refers to fixed expressions or collocations, a common concept in language learning.  
• "van werkwoorden en preposities" shows the typical Dutch use of "van" to indicate relationships, similar to "of" in English.

• Extra Sentences:  
  - "Morgen leren we over de geschiedenis van Nederland." (Tomorrow we learn about the history of the Netherlands.)  
  - "Ze werken aan een project over duurzame energie." (They are working on a project about sustainable energy.)  
  - "Hij geeft een presentatie over vaste uitdrukkingen." (He is giving a presentation about fixed expressions.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Vandaag bespreken we de regels van de Nederlandse taal." (Today we discuss the rules of the Dutch language.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of hashtags like "#dutchgrammar" in the sentence suggests it might be from an online or social media context, where learners share resources and tips. Dutch learners often use online platforms to connect and share learning strategies.

sentences.nl: Waar is het feestje? — Hier is het feestje!
sentences.en: Where's the party? — Here's the party!

sentences.nl: En in Nederland is de traditie:, wie jarig is trakteert!
sentences.en: And in the Netherlands, the tradition is: whoever has a birthday treats!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• And in the Netherlands is the tradition: who birthday has treats!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The word "wie" is used here to mean "whoever" or "the one who," indicating the person who has the birthday.  
• "Jarig" is an adjective derived from "jaar" (year) and is used to describe someone who is having their birthday.  
• "Trakteert" is the third person singular form of "trakteren," which means "to treat" or "to give a treat."

• Examples:  
  - "Wie het eerst komt, het eerst maalt." (First come, first served.)  
  - "Wie niet horen wil, moet voelen." (Those who will not listen must feel.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Wie vroeg opstaat, heeft meer aan zijn dag." (Whoever gets up early, gets more out of their day.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is customary for the person who is celebrating their birthday to bring treats for their colleagues or classmates, rather than them receiving gifts or treats from others.

sentences.nl: Een ‘prikkertje’ is een stukje kaas met een vlaggetje.
sentences.en: A "prikkertje" is a piece of cheese with a little flag.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A 'prikkertje' is a piece of cheese with a little flag.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een" is an indefinite article meaning "a" or "an."  
• "Prikkertje" is a diminutive form of "prikker," indicating a small version, often used to refer to a toothpick or snack on a stick.  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of "zijn," meaning "is."  
• "Een stukje kaas" means "a piece of cheese," where "stukje" is the diminutive form of "stuk," meaning "piece."  
• "Met" is a preposition meaning "with."  
• "Een vlaggetje" is "a little flag," with "vlaggetje" being the diminutive of "vlag," which means "flag."

Extra Examples:  
• "Een kopje koffie is altijd lekker." (A cup of coffee is always nice.)  
• "Een huisje aan zee zou perfect zijn." (A little house by the sea would be perfect.)  
• "Ik heb een cadeautje voor je." (I have a little gift for you.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een 'bitterballetje' is een gefrituurd hapje met vlees." (A 'bitterball' is a fried snack with meat.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The "prikkertje" is a common snack at Dutch parties, often consisting of a small cube of cheese and a pickled onion or piece of gherkin, all skewered with a toothpick that sometimes has a small decorative flag.

sentences.nl: Met verder nog een knakworstje,, een druif,, een uitje, of een augurk.
sentences.en: With furthermore a little sausage, a grape, a small onion, or a pickle.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• With further still a small sausage, a grape, an onion, or a pickle.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Met" is a preposition meaning "with."  
• "Verder nog" is a common phrase meaning "furthermore" or "in addition to."  
• The nouns "knakworstje," "druif," "uitje," and "augurk" are all singular and preceded by an indefinite article "een" (a/an).  
• The use of commas and "of" (or) indicates a list of options or additions.

Examples:  
- "Met verder nog een kopje koffie." (With furthermore a cup of coffee.)  
- "Hij wil verder nog een toetje." (He wants furthermore a dessert.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Met verder nog een kop thee, een koekje, of een stukje chocolade. (With furthermore a cup of tea, a cookie, or a piece of chocolate.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Knakworstje" often refers to a type of small, smoked sausage similar to a hot dog, commonly eaten in the Netherlands as a snack or part of a simple meal.

sentences.nl: De studenten hebben een cadeautje voor Marieke.
sentences.en: The students have a present for Marieke.

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Please Marieke, from heart congratulations!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Alsjeblieft" is a polite way to say "please" or "here you go" when giving something. It can also be used to grab someone's attention politely.  
• "Van harte gefeliciteerd" means "congratulations from the heart" and is a common way to wish someone a heartfelt happy birthday or congratulate them on an achievement. "Van harte" literally means "from the heart" and "gefeliciteerd" means "congratulated."  
• "Gefeliciteerd" is a past participle used here as an adjective or an exclamation.  

Extra phrases:  
- "Alsjeblieft, hier is je koffie." (Please, here is your coffee.)  
- "Van harte welkom!" (A warm welcome!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Van harte bedankt voor je hulp!" (Heartfelt thanks for your help!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common to congratulate not just the person celebrating a birthday but also their family members and close friends. This reflects the importance of social bonds and family in Dutch culture.

sentences.en: On behalf of all the students.

sentences.nl: Mag ik het uitpakken? — Ja natuurlijk!
sentences.en: Can I unpack it? — Yes, of course!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• May I it unpack? — Yes, naturally!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Mag ik" means "May I" and is used for asking permission. The verb "mogen" is modal and comes first in questions.  
• "Het uitpakken" means "to unpack it," where "het" is the direct object, and "uitpakken" is the verb "to unpack."  
• "Ja natuurlijk!" is a common affirmative response meaning "Yes, naturally!" or "Of course!"

• Examples:  
  - Mag ik naar het toilet? (May I go to the toilet?)  
  - Mag ik je helpen? (May I help you?)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Mag ik hier zitten? (May I sit here?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's polite to ask for permission before doing something that might affect others, such as unpacking a gift in someone else's home.

sentences.nl: Een bon voor de kapper hier in het dorp!
sentences.en: A voucher for the hairdresser here in the village!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A voucher for the hairdresser here in the village!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een bon" (a voucher) is an indefinite noun phrase.  
• "Voor de kapper" (for the hairdresser) uses the preposition "voor" to indicate purpose or intended recipient.  
• "Hier in het dorp" (here in the village) combines "hier" (here) with a location phrase, using "in" to specify place.  

Extra sentences:  
• "Een cadeau voor de leraar." (A gift for the teacher.)  
• "Hij woont hier in de stad." (He lives here in the city.)  
• "Een ticket voor het concert." (A ticket for the concert.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een kaartje voor de bioscoop hier in de buurt." (A ticket for the cinema here in the neighborhood.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Often, small communities in the Netherlands will have local shops and services such as a "kapper" (hairdresser) which can be central to village life.

sentences.nl: Ik ben erg blij met jullie cadeau.
sentences.en: I am very happy with your gift.

sentences.nl: Ondertussen staat Martin buiten bij de Summer School.
sentences.en: Meanwhile, Martin is outside at the Summer School.
He is going to surprise Marieke.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He goes Marieke surprise.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence uses the verb "gaat" which is the third person singular form of "gaan" (to go). In this context, it indicates a future intention, similar to the English "going to" future tense.  
• "Verrassen" is the infinitive form of the verb "to surprise." In Dutch, the infinitive often comes at the end of the sentence in constructions like this.  
• "Hij gaat naar de markt." (He is going to the market.)  
• "Zij gaat een boek lezen." (She is going to read a book.)  
• "Wij gaan morgen zwemmen." (We are going to swim tomorrow.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij gaat haar moeder bellen. (She is going to call her mother.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, surprises, especially for birthdays or special occasions, are common and often involve small gatherings or thoughtful gestures.

sentences.nl: Hij verlangt naar haar, want hij is verliefd op haar.
sentences.en: He longs for her because he is in love with her.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He longs for her, because he is in love with her.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hij verlangt naar haar": "verlangen naar" is a fixed phrase meaning "to long for."  
• "want": This is a coordinating conjunction meaning "because" that doesn't affect the word order.  
• "is verliefd op": "verliefd op" is a fixed phrase meaning "in love with."  

• Extra phrases/sentences:  
  - Zij verlangt naar vakantie. (She longs for a holiday.)  
  - Ik ben verliefd op jou. (I am in love with you.)  
  - Hij is moe, want hij heeft niet geslapen. (He is tired because he hasn’t slept.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij verlangt naar de zomer, want ze houdt van het warme weer. (She longs for the summer because she loves the warm weather.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch-speaking cultures, expressing feelings openly, like being "verliefd op" someone, is generally considered normal and is often encouraged in personal relationships.

sentences.nl: En hij denkt dat Marieke ook op hem verliefd is.
sentences.en: And he thinks that Marieke is also in love with him.

sentences.nl: Hij wacht op een seintje van Lars.
sentences.en: He is waiting for a signal from Lars.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• He waits for a signal from Lars.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Hij wacht op" is a separable verb structure where "wachten" (to wait) is combined with the preposition "op" to mean "to wait for."  
• "Een seintje" means "a signal," where "seintje" is a diminutive of "sein" (signal). Diminutives often convey informality or smallness.  
• "Van Lars" indicates possession, literally "from Lars."

Examples:  
• Zij kijkt uit naar de zomer. (She looks forward to the summer.)  
• We wachten op de bus. (We are waiting for the bus.)  
• Hij vraagt om hulp. (He asks for help.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij wacht op een telefoontje van haar moeder. (She is waiting for a phone call from her mother.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Seintje" can imply a small, informal message or cue, often used in casual communication to indicate waiting for a quick reply or confirmation.

sentences.nl: Lars stuurt een sms’je naar Martin.
sentences.en: Lars sends a text message to Martin.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Lars sends a text message to Martin.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The verb "stuurt" is the third person singular present tense of "sturen," meaning "to send."  
• "Een sms’je" is a diminutive form of "sms," meaning "a text message." The diminutive indicates something small or endearing.  
• "Naar" is a preposition meaning "to" in this context, used to indicate direction towards someone or something.

• Extra Examples:  
  - "Hij stuurt een brief naar zijn oma." (He sends a letter to his grandma.)  
  - "Zij stuurt een uitnodiging naar al haar vrienden." (She sends an invitation to all her friends.)  
  - "Ik stuur een e-mail naar de leraar." (I send an email to the teacher.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Maria stuurt een kaartje naar haar zus. (Maria sends a card to her sister.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• "Sms'je" is a commonly used term for a text message in Dutch. Despite the popularity of messaging apps, the term is still widely recognized.

sentences.nl: Marieke, van harte gefeliciteerd met je verjaardag!
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke, of heart congratulations with your birthday!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The phrase "van harte" is an idiomatic expression meaning "wholeheartedly" or "sincerely." It is commonly used in congratulatory contexts.  
• "Gefeliciteerd" is the past participle of "feliciteren," meaning "to congratulate." In Dutch, it's often used as a standalone congratulatory expression.  
• The preposition "met" is used here to indicate the occasion being celebrated, similar to "on" in English.

• Examples:  
  - "Van harte welkom!" (Hearty welcome!)  
  - "Gefeliciteerd met je diploma!" (Congratulations on your diploma!)  
  - "Ik ben blij met het resultaat." (I am happy with the result.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Sophie, van harte gefeliciteerd met je nieuwe baan!" (Sophie, heartfelt congratulations on your new job!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to congratulate not just the person celebrating their birthday but also their family and friends.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin gives 3 kisses to Marieke.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Geeft" is the third-person singular form of the verb "geven," meaning "to give." Dutch verbs change form based on the subject.  
• The structure "geeft...aan" indicates giving something to someone, similar to "gives...to" in English.  
• The number "3" is used as an adjective describing "kussen" (kisses). In Dutch, numbers precede nouns without additional articles.  
• Example sentences:  
  - "Ze geeft een cadeau aan haar vriend." (She gives a gift to her friend.)  
  - "Hij stuurt een brief aan zijn ouders." (He sends a letter to his parents.)  
  - "Wij geven de hond eten." (We give the dog food.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Lisa geeft een boek aan haar zus." (Lisa gives a book to her sister.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it is common to greet friends and family with three kisses on the cheek, alternating cheeks. This is a form of greeting or farewell among close acquaintances.

sentences.en: That's how it should be done in the Netherlands.

sentences.nl: Marieke, hier is mijn cadeautje voor jou.
sentences.en: Marieke, here is my gift for you.

sentences.nl: Een knuffel…, in de vorm van de maan.
sentences.en: A hug..., in the shape of the moon.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• A hug…, in the shape of the moon.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Een knuffel" means "a hug" or "a stuffed animal," depending on context.  
• "In de vorm van" means "in the shape of," a common phrase for describing shapes or forms.  
• "De maan" is "the moon," with "de" as the definite article for singular common gender nouns.

• Examples:  
  - "Een taart in de vorm van een hart." (A cake in the shape of a heart.)  
  - "Een gebouw in de vorm van een piramide." (A building in the shape of a pyramid.)  
  - "Hij gaf me een knuffel." (He gave me a hug.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Een lamp in de vorm van een ster." (A lamp in the shape of a star.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The phrase "in de vorm van de maan" could refer to a popular design trend in home decor or children's toys, where objects are styled after celestial shapes like moons and stars, often popular in Dutch nurseries.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• What original !?!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Wat" is used here as an exclamatory expression, similar to "How" or "What" in English when expressing surprise or admiration.  
• "Origineel" is an adjective meaning "original" and is used to describe something unique or creative.

• Examples:  
  - Wat leuk! (How nice!)  
  - Wat een verrassing! (What a surprise!)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Wat spannend! (How exciting!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, the use of "Wat" followed by an adjective is common in exclamations to express a strong emotion or reaction. This can be used in both positive and negative contexts, depending on the adjective used.

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

vandaag.spelling: The combination 'aa' in 'vandaag' indicates a long /aː/ sound, typical for Dutch vowels.
vandaag.fast: The final /x/ in 'vandaag' may be softened or dropped in rapid speech, especially if followed by a vowel.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

dutchgrammar.fast: In connected speech, the final /r/ in ‘grammar’ may become less pronounced or vocalized.

les.spelling: Short /ɛ/ in a closed syllable followed by a voiceless /s/.
les.fast: In rapid speech, the final /s/ in ‘les is’ may become voiceless between vowels, leading to a pronunciation like [lɛsɪs].

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

waar.spelling: The 'aa' in 'waar' represents a long /aː/ sound, typical for open syllables.
waar.fast: In connected speech, the /r/ in 'waar is' may be more relaxed or even dropped, leading to a smoother transition between words.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

nederland.spelling: The open syllable 'nee-' indicates a long /eː/, while '-der-' and '-land' reflect standard Dutch vowel and consonant patterns.
nederland.fast: In rapid speech, the final /t/ in 'nederland' may be unreleased or slightly assimilated before a following consonant.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

wat.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in closed syllables.
wat.fast: In connected speech, 'wat' often reduces to /wət/ or even /wə/ before vowels.

uit.fast: In rapid speech, the diphthong /œyt/ can be slightly reduced to /œt/.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

hoe.spelling: The vowel sound /uː/ in 'hoe' is represented by the letters 'oe', a common Dutch spelling for this sound.
